passage:
The plotter jammed at 6:10 pm, twenty minutes before the municipal submission, and Swati simply sat down on the print-room floor of the architecture firm.
She didn't decide to cry. It just came, heavy and shaking, the kind she couldn't stop by breathing.
Yogesh, her team lead, found her there. He crouched a little distance away. "I'll email the drawings myself. You're going home."
"I can do it," she said, and couldn't even stand.
In the cab she stared at her hands. Three years without missing a deadline, and now this. Pathetic, she thought.
At home she slept fourteen hours without waking. The next morning her body felt like wet sand.
Yogesh had messaged: "Submission went through. Take tomorrow off. Let's talk on Thursday about your load, no pressure."
She read it twice and felt ashamed and, underneath that, strangely grateful.

qa.q: How long did Swati sleep after she got home?
qa.a: She slept fourteen hours without waking.

qa.q: What did Swati think of herself in the cab, and why?
qa.a: She thought she was pathetic, because after three years without missing a deadline, breaking down felt like failure.

qa.q: What turning point does Yogesh's message open for Swati?
qa.a: It lets her rest properly and then talk honestly on Thursday about her load, treating the crash as a signal rather than a failure.

qa.q: What might Yogesh have felt finding Swati on the print-room floor?
qa.a: He may have been shaken to see a reliable team member unable to stand, and chose to take the task off her and send her home instead of pushing the deadline.

grounding: Shows a young professional breaking down before a deadline and sleeping fourteen hours, a crash that feels like failure but is the body forcing rest.

passage:
Thomas,
I'm writing this from bed at 3 pm on a Monday. The quarterly deck was due at ten. I set four alarms. I heard every one of them, and I could not make my body get up. Not lazy-couldn't. Couldn't, like my arms were filled with sand.
At eleven I finally messaged my manager: "Unwell, can't make it today." Then I cried for an hour, because I have never, ever done that.
It feels like I've failed at the one thing I'm known for. You know me, the 2 am edits person.
But lying here I keep thinking how I've been saying "I'll rest after this project" since March. Maybe my body just stopped waiting for me to agree.
I'm scared of what I'll say to my manager tomorrow.
Can you call me tonight?
Noor

qa.q: How many alarms did Noor set?
qa.a: Noor set four alarms.

qa.q: Why does Noor feel like a failure after missing the deadline?
qa.a: Noor is upset because Noor is known for 2 am edits and has never missed work like this, so staying in bed feels like failing at the one thing Noor is known for.

qa.q: What could Noor do before facing the manager tomorrow?
qa.a: Noor could rest today, talk it through with Thomas tonight and plan to be honest about months of overwork; if the heavy tiredness keeps going, a doctor visit would help.

qa.q: What might Thomas feel when this letter arrives?
qa.a: Thomas may be worried to hear that a friend who never misses deadlines couldn't get out of bed, and glad to be the one Noor reached out to.

grounding: Illustrates being unable to get out of bed for a Monday deadline, feeling it as failure while sensing the body has enforced overdue rest.

passage:
Jeevan,
You asked why I missed the release on Monday. Here's the truth.
On Friday I came home at eleven and slept in my clothes. I didn't wake up until Sunday afternoon. Not once. On Monday, the alarm went off at seven, and I lay there and couldn't move. Not wouldn't. Couldn't. I cried like a kid, holding my phone, looking at the work notifications piling up.
I felt like the biggest failure. Everyone else manages. I've always managed.
My mother made me see a doctor on Tuesday. She said it sounded like my body finally took the rest I kept refusing it. I'm starting to think she's right.
Dhruv

qa.q: When did Dhruv wake up after sleeping in his clothes?
qa.a: Sunday afternoon.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he couldn't get out of bed on Monday?
qa.a: Dhruv felt like a failure, overwhelmed and ashamed, crying while notifications piled up.

qa.q: What turning point came after the crash?
qa.a: Seeing a doctor on Tuesday and starting to see the crash as the body enforcing rest, not a personal failure.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Jeevan may feel worried and sympathetic, and glad Dhruv told the truth instead of hiding it.

grounding: Shows a young worker who sleeps through a weekend and cannot get up for a Monday deadline, feeling like a failure as the body enforces rest.

passage:
Tanuja, you asked what happened last month. Okay. I'll tell you straight.
For a year I'd been working late every night. Then one Monday, the big client deadline, I woke up and just... couldn't. I lay there. My body felt like wet cement. I watched the clock go past nine, then ten. My phone kept buzzing. I cried so hard I couldn't breathe properly.
I thought, that's it. I'm a failure. I've let everyone down.
My flatmate called my sister, and my sister took me to the doctor that afternoon. The doctor said something I still think about: "You didn't fail. Your body made you stop because you wouldn't."
I'm Nazia. I'm better now. Slowly.

qa.q: What did Nazia say the body felt like?
qa.a: Like wet cement.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling as the clock went past nine and ten?
qa.a: Nazia felt like a failure, overwhelmed and guilty for letting everyone down.

qa.q: What helped Nazia after the crash?
qa.a: The flatmate calling Nazia's sister, who took Nazia to the doctor that afternoon.

qa.q: What might the flatmate have been feeling that morning?
qa.a: The flatmate was probably frightened and worried, which is why they called Nazia's sister.

grounding: Shows a young worker unable to get out of bed for a Monday deadline, feeling like a failure, and a doctor calling it the body's forced rest.

passage:
Friday: Santosh stayed at the office until midnight finishing slides. He skipped dinner again. On the bus home he felt his heart racing for no reason.
Saturday and Sunday: He slept. And slept. His roommate Abhinav knocked at noon on Saturday, then at dinner, then on Sunday. Santosh mumbled something and turned over.
Monday: The alarm rang at 6:30. Santosh stared at the ceiling. His deadline was at ten. He tried to sit up and couldn't. Tears slid into his ears. I've failed, he thought. Abhinav came in, saw him, and sat on the edge of the bed. "Bro, I'm calling your manager. And then we're going to the doctor."

qa.q: What time did Santosh's alarm ring on Monday?
What was Santosh feeling on Monday morning?
qa.a: He felt like a failure, ashamed and overwhelmed, unable to sit up for his deadline.

qa.q: What turning point does Abhinav create?
qa.a: He calls the manager and takes Santosh to the doctor, treating the crash as a need for rest and care.

qa.q: What is Abhinav experiencing over the weekend?
qa.a: Abhinav seems increasingly worried as Santosh keeps sleeping, and on Monday decides to act.

grounding: Shows a young worker crashing over a weekend and unable to rise for a Monday deadline, feeling like failure while his body forces rest.

passage: "Jomon, sit. You've been here till ten every night this month, so I'm going to tell you something I don't tell many people. When I was twenty-five, in my first design job, I said yes to everything for a whole year. One Monday, the day of the biggest client deadline of my life, I woke up and could not get out of bed. I don't mean I didn't want to. My arms would not lift the blanket. I cried, I slept, I woke, I slept, through the whole day and into Tuesday. My roommate Mercy called my manager and then called a doctor. I felt like the worst failure in the world. Months later I understood it differently: my body took the rest I had refused it for a year. So this is your Usha ma'am telling you: go home at six today."

qa.q: What happened on the Monday of the big deadline?
qa.a: Usha woke up and could not get out of bed.

qa.q: How did young Usha feel about the crash at first?
qa.a: She felt like the worst failure in the world, ashamed that her body gave out on deadline day.

qa.q: What choice earlier in the story might have prevented young Usha's crash?
qa.a: Saying no to some of that year's requests, or telling the manager about the load before the deadline, might have prevented it.

qa.q: What might that Monday have been like for Mercy?
qa.a: Mercy was likely frightened to see Usha unable to get up, and acted by calling the manager and a doctor.

grounding: Shows a young designer crashing on a deadline Monday after a year of overwork, feeling it as failure, later seeing it as the body forcing rest.
